options: A single running program managed by an operating system
Software that emulates a complete computer, able to run its own full operating system
A physical server dedicated to one application
A type of network cable used in data centers
questions.explain: A VM emulates an entire computer — virtual CPU, RAM, storage, and network interface — convincingly enough for a full, separate operating system to run inside it.

options: Writing application code for the guest operating system
Creating virtual machines, allocating real hardware to each, and keeping them isolated from one another
Replacing the need for an operating system inside a VM
Physically connecting servers with network cables
questions.explain: The hypervisor is the software layer responsible for creating VMs, handing out slices of real CPU/RAM/storage to each one, and isolating them from each other.

questions.q: What distinguishes a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor from a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor?
options: Type 1 runs directly on hardware with no host OS; Type 2 runs as an application on top of a host OS
Type 1 only works on laptops; Type 2 only works in data centers
Type 1 cannot create more than one VM; Type 2 can create unlimited VMs
There is no functional difference between the two
questions.explain: Type 1 hypervisors run directly on the physical hardware (the data center/production standard), while Type 2 hypervisors run as an ordinary application on top of a regular host operating system (common for laptops and testing).

questions.q: Why did virtualization become common for businesses running multiple applications?
options: It was required by law in most countries
Dedicating one mostly-idle physical server per application wasted hardware capacity, which virtualization lets you consolidate
Physical servers stopped being manufactured
Virtual machines run applications faster than any physical server ever could
questions.explain: Before virtualization, a business often bought one physical server per application, most of which sat mostly idle. Virtualization lets one host run many isolated VMs, each sized to what it actually needs.

questions.q: When a customer "spins up a server in the cloud," what is actually happening underneath?
options: A brand-new physical server is manufactured and shipped
The customer is requesting a new virtual machine from the cloud provider's hypervisor layer
The customer gains direct physical access to a data center
No operating system is involved at any point
questions.explain: Public cloud providers run massive data centers of physical servers under hypervisors and rent out individual VMs on demand — the customer never sees or touches the underlying physical hardware.
